newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic backs down but Serbia protests to go on.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic backs down but Serbia protests to go on.

text.p: Serbia's authoritarian President Slobodan Milosevic, bowing to pressure from relentless pro-democracy protests, said on Tuesday that opposition victories in disputed local elections must be reinstated.

The austere socialist leader, who had virtually ignored massive street rallies and then unleashed his paramilitary police on demonstrators two days ago, asked parliament to restore November's election outcome.
Opposition coalition leaders gave the news a cautious welcome, but vowed to continue their rallies -- now in their 77th day -- until media were liberalised and other democratic reforms implemented.
"It is up to Milosevic whether we will fight at democratic elections or in the streets," opposition coalition politician Vuk Draskovic told cheering supporters in downtown Belgrade.
Socialist (SPS) hardliners close to Milosevic had annulled the November 17 ballot in 14 cities and towns, citing "irregularities" which the opposition denounced as fraud.
The SPS re-ran the elections, but the opposition shunned them and pressure intensified both on Serbia's streets and diplomatic corridors abroad for the SPS to concede defeat.

After two days of police attacks on largely peaceful demonstrators that prompted fears of emergency rule, Milosevic instructed his Prime Minister, Mirko Marjanovic, to have parliament uphold the election outcome.
Within hours Marjanovic told state radio and television that a draft law reinstating the disputed part of the local election results would probably be submitted to parliament on Wednesday.
The Yugoslav news agency Tanjug reported a statement from Belgrade's SPS leadership welcoming Milosevic's decision.
"It will provide conditions for the citizens of Serbia to return to normal life and work," the SPS statement said.
Diplomats and domestic political analysts said Milosevic's capitulation to the Serbian pro-democracy movement was not a total surprise but the question was why it took 77 days.
Authoritative political sources said he was using that time preparing for a showdown with diehards in his party.
"Milosevic's concession is more a result of the moderates prevailing over the hardliners (in the SPS)," one source said.

"In keeping with its constiutional competence, I propose that the Serbian government submit to parliament a draft emergency law which will proclaim as final results of a part of local elections in Serbia in keeping with the findings of the OSCE (factfinding) mission," Milosevic said in his letter to the prime minister. The 'part' referred to those results annulled by the authorities.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe had verified the opposition claim to election triumphs.
Eighty thousand opposition demonstrators massed in central Belgrade cheered wildly when told of Milosevic's climbdown.
Earlier, Reuters photographers saw some marchers express contempt by barking at police and tossing bones at their feet.
Others shouted "Ustashe", a reference to the Croatian fascist puppet government set up by Nazi occupiers in Zagreb during World War Two.
Oppositon co-leader Zoran Djindjic, wary of possible Socialist subterfuge, said protests would not end yet.

"We will continue them until all (municipal) councillor mandates are verified, until freedom of the media is established, and until responsibility is established of all those who took part in the vote theft and brutal beating up of citizens," he told the raucous throng.

Earlier in the day, the 54-nation OSCE, from which the Yugoslav federation comprising Serbia and Montenegro has been suspended, appealed urgently for dialogue between Milosevic and the opposition coalition, Zajedno.
Municipal bodies have limited powers in Serbia, but they control regional media, especially television. Parliamentary and presidential elections are due by the end of 1997.
Diplomats cautioned that the crisis was not over.
"A danger is that the opposition, buoyed by victory, would not get off the streets as promised and keep pressing for demands, like his (Milosevic's) resignation," said one diplomat.
